props.title: Jack Frost
props.initialSlug: Killer snowman terrorizes small mountain town

sections.content: Jack Frost stands as a notorious entry in the killer snowman subgenre of horror-comedy, distinctly different from the 1998 Michael Keaton family film of the same name. The film follows a serial killer who gets genetically mutated into a murderous snowman after a chemical accident, creating a bizarre blend of slasher tropes and winter imagery. This fits into the wave of self-aware 90s horror like Scream (1996) and I Know What You Did Last Summer (1997), but takes a more deliberately campy approach similar to Leprechaun (1993) and Puppet Master (1989).

sections.content: The late 1990s saw a surge in deliberately campy direct-to-video horror, with Uncle Sam (1996) and Pinocchio's Revenge (1996) mining similar territory of turning innocent figures into killers. Jack Frost distinguishes itself through its commitment to ridiculous snow-themed kills and groan-worthy winter puns. The film spawned a sequel, Jack Frost 2: Revenge of the Mutant Killer Snowman (2000), doubling down on the absurdist humor.

The practical effects, while clearly low-budget, show creative ingenuity in bringing a murderous snowman to life before widespread CGI adoption. This puts it in company with other practical effects-driven horror comedies like Killer Klowns from Outer Space (1988) and Critters (1986), where the charm comes from seeing how filmmakers solve technical challenges with limited resources. sections.content: Jack Frost represents the evolution of horror-comedy from the 1980s slasher satires like Student Bodies (1981) to more postmodern takes. While films like Scary Movie (1999) would later parody horror conventions more directly, Jack Frost creates its own absurdist mythology while acknowledging genre tropes. This approach influenced later cult horror-comedies like Thankskilling (2009) and Rubber (2010).
